## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Machine Learning — SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet: "Programme d'approfondissement — Bases de l'Apprentissage Automatique" (occurrence: "Foundations of Machine Learning")
  Code                    MDC_51006_EP
  Team and workload       Responsible (sheet): Erwan Le Pennec & Jesse Read; responsible of the 2026-2027 occurrence: Erwan Le Pennec · teaching team: Arunava Gantait, Thierry Klein, Paul Mangold, Poyraz Yilan · 36 h in person (lecture / small-class split not displayed; max enrollment 144) · 4.5 ECTS · assessment: a final exam (official description) · language of instruction: English · the methodological foundation of the program: supervised and unsupervised learning, from least squares to boosting, together with the accompanying generalization theory.
  Status in the program   [Mandatory]{.badge .mandatory} M1 · S1 / period 1 — X-3A-P1 (fall semester, from 17/09/26 to 18/12/26)
  ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: engineer who already fitted a sklearn model / MNIST-like MLP and wants to understand *why* it generalizes (or not) — without opening on VC dimension. **Empirical first**: visible overfitting on a train/test split, ridge that "calibrates" coefficients, a forest that works when linear fails.

Mandatory module: methodological foundation — learning from data, and under what conditions it works. Supervised (least squares → boosting), unsupervised, generalization theory. This is what separates understanding models from calling a library. Downstream LLGA (DL, NLP, Graph ML, RL) reuses this vocabulary.

### What you will be able to do

-   Frame a learning problem: risk, empirical risk, hypotheses, bias-variance trade-off.
-   Implement and tune linear regression, ridge/Lasso regularization, logistic regression and SVMs, justifying every choice.
-   Use kernels to move to the nonlinear setting and understand what a "reproducing kernel Hilbert space" brings in practice.
-   Choose between trees, random forests and boosting (gradient boosting) according to the nature of the data and the interpretability constraint, and explain a tree ensemble with Shapley values and permutation importance.
-   Conduct a complete unsupervised analysis: k-means, Gaussian mixture and EM, PCA and dimensionality reduction.
-   State and exploit generalization bounds to argue for a model's performance on new data.
-   Build a rigorous evaluation pipeline: splits, cross-validation, adapted metrics, per-group metrics and fairness criteria, honest comparison of two models, scaling up.
-   Read an academic or industrial ML paper and identify the underlying statistical framework.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

**Official objectives** (paraphrased from the description published on SynapseS): machine learning is the discipline that designs algorithms allowing computers to learn from data, automatically extract complex patterns from them and derive intelligent decisions from them. The course focuses on the *methodology underlying supervised and unsupervised learning*, with a particular emphasis on the *mathematical formulation of the algorithms* and on how they can be *implemented and used in practice*; to this end it presents the necessary tools from optimization theory.

Proofs are not done in lecture: some are done in labs, others are given in a document; each lab ends with a numerical exercise in Python. **Official assessment: a final exam.**

No session-by-session programme is displayed (the "Descriptif & programme" tab of the sheet is empty); the following table maps every element of the official description to our chapters.

### Where this course fits in the program

This mandatory module of Year 1 · Period 1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS) is the hinge of the program: it assumes the two refresher modules are completed, [Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html) (probability, basic inequalities, estimation, tests, linear regression) and [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html) (Python, NumPy, complexity). The refreshers do not teach optimization: the opening chapter "Review" supplies it (gradient descent, convexity, duality), together with Hoeffding's inequality and the entropy and KL divergence used throughout.

The official 2026-2027 sheet displays no prerequisites (its tab is empty), but the emphasis on mathematical formulation and Python labs presupposes precisely these two foundations. The course unit is moreover shared with the engineering cycle (X), the MJH, MPRI and CCSN master's programs and the other MScT tracks ViCAI and TRAI — hence a course tailored to advanced scientific profiles.

Downstream, it feeds everything else in the program. [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) immediately follows by revisiting the perceptron and gradient descent; [Emerging Subjects in ML](../m1p1-emerging-ml/index.html) reuses SGD and generalization theory for distributed learning. The [Statistical Learning Theory](../m1p1-statistical-learning-theory/index.html) notes deepen chapter 8 up to VC bounds and Rademacher complexity; that course is not in the LLGA 1 – S1 list (it is still offered in other tracks), and its notes are kept on this site for reference. The chapter on evaluation, big data and pipelines directly prepares the projects and applied modules of Period 2, from NLP to Graph ML.

The chapter "Research at CMAP and LIX (Le Pennec, Read)" presents the research of Erwan Le Pennec (CMAP) and Jesse Read (LIX): it is a gateway to internships and possible PhD topics from the end of M1.

### Course outline

-   **Review: optimization, concentration and information**: gradient, convexity, concentration inequalities, entropy and KL divergence, Lagrangian duality — L3 tools, immediately mobilized.
-   **The statistical framework of learning**: risk, empirical minimization, bias-variance — the constitution of the problem.
-   **Linear regression and regularization**: the reference model and the first answer to overfitting.
-   **Classification: logistic, SVM and naive Bayes**: margins, losses, decision boundaries, generative versus discriminative modelling.
-   **Evaluation, big data and pipelines**: operational rigor — metrics, validation, scaling up.
-   **Kernels and RKHS**: linearizing the nonlinear via the kernel embedding.
-   **Trees, forests, boosting**: the still-essential family on tabular data, in companies as in competitions.
-   **Unsupervised: k-means, EM, PCA**: segmenting and compressing without labels.
-   **Generalization theory**: why (and when) the empirical error announces the true error.
-   **Research at CMAP and LIX (Le Pennec, Read)**: research at CMAP and LIX, from forests to ensembles, and possible internship topics.

### How to study this module

-   First secure the review: the opening chapter gathers the L3 optimization and concentration tools, which the [Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html) does not cover, and the entropy and KL divergence met in its section 9.3. The refresher's probability and estimation chapters are assumed: if an exercise there resists you, handle it before moving on.
-   Follow the chapter order: every model family (linear, kernels, trees) is taken up again by generalization theory, which only makes sense after them.
-   Reimplement at least once each familiar model (ridge regression, k-means, a tree) in NumPy before using scikit-learn.
-   Do the paper exercises on bounds and bias-variance: these are the most discriminating questions in the assessments.
-   Build a complete end-to-end mini-pipeline on a real dataset as soon as chapter 4 is done: this is what recruiters expect, and every later model family plugs into it.
-   Keep the chapter "Research at CMAP and LIX (Le Pennec, Read)" as an orientation signal: it announces internship topics. For more theory after chapter 8, the [Statistical Learning Theory](../m1p1-statistical-learning-theory/index.html) notes are kept on this site for reference (that course is not in the LLGA list).

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} Whether you aim at LLM×graph deployment or a PhD, the founding question remains that of this module: under what conditions does a model learned on past data generalize? Transformers, GNNs, systems — answers to that question. We start from numbers (split, train vs test error), not from VC.
:::

### Notation {#notation}

**Deviations from the site-wide conventions** ([notation page](../../notation/index.html)). Chapter 2 writes $p$ for the number of features, as regression textbooks do. Chapter 9 writes $L$ for the number of labels, as the multi-label literature does. The Lagrangian of sections 0.4 and 3.2 is written $\mathcal{L}$; it is minimized over the primal variables.

Everywhere else the page follows the [site-wide conventions](../../notation/index.html):

-   **Data**: a sample $D_n = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ drawn iid from $\mathbb{P}$, with $n$ examples and $d$ features, and $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$.
-   **Losses and risks**: a loss $\ell(\hat y, y)$ is written prediction first; $\mathcal{R}(f)$ is the risk, $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f)$ the empirical risk, and $F(\theta)$ an objective minimized over parameters.
-   **Reserved letters**: $\eta$ is a learning rate, or the inverse temperature of exponential weights; $L$ is a smoothness (Lipschitz) constant, or the graph Laplacian $L = D - A$ in graph examples; the bound maximized by EM is written $\mathrm{ELBO}$.

## 0. Review: optimization, concentration and information tools {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used throughout the module
:::

-   **Gradient**: $\nabla f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ points in the direction of steepest ascent; for $f(x)=\frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$, $\nabla f(x) = A^\top(Ax - b)$.
-   **Convexity**: $f$ is convex if
    $$
    f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda) f(y).
    $$
    A local minimum of a convex function is global — the reason so many ML losses are designed convex.
-   **Gradient descent**: $x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta \nabla f(x_t)$, convergence $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ for a step $\eta < 1/L$ ($L$ = Lipschitz constant of the gradient).
-   **Symmetric matrices**: diagonalizable ($A = Q \Lambda Q^\top$, $Q$ orthogonal); $A \succeq 0$ (positive) iff all its eigenvalues are $\geq 0$. For a symmetric matrix, $\sup_{\|v\| \leq 1} v^\top A v = \lambda_{\max}(A)$ (Rayleigh quotient) — the hidden tool of PCA (chapter 7).
::::

### 0.1. Why concentration inequalities in an ML course?

All of generalization theory (chapter 8) rests on one simple question: is the empirical risk $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f)$, computed on $n$ examples, close to the true risk $\mathcal{R}(f)$? The answer is given by concentration inequalities — results of probability analysis that we use here as a black box, proved once and for all.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.1 — Markov's inequality]{.tag} Let $Z \geq 0$ be an integrable random variable. For every $t > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}(Z \geq t) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[Z]}{t}.$$

::: proof
Writing $Z = Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z \geq t\} + Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z < t\}$ and noting that $Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z \geq t\} \geq t\,\mathbf{1}\{Z \geq t\}$, monotonicity of the expectation gives $\mathbb{E}[Z] \geq t\,\mathbb{P}(Z \geq t)$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Chebyshev's inequality]{.tag} Let $X$ have finite variance. For every $t > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}\big(|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \geq t\big) \leq \frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{t^2}.$$

::: proof
Apply Markov to $Z = (X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2 \geq 0$ with threshold $t^2$ and note that $\{|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \geq t\} = \{Z \geq t^2\}$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Chebyshev gives a $1/(nt^2)$ decay for a mean of $n$ variables: usable but slow, and with no exponential control. The extra ingredient — **independence** — provides the exponential magic.

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 — Hoeffding's inequality]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent with $X_i \in [a_i, b_i]$ almost surely and $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$. For every $t > 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\big(S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \geq t\big) \leq \exp\!\Big(-\,\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (b_i - a_i)^2}\Big),
$$
and the same bound holds for the deviation $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{E}[S_n] - S_n \geq t)$. In particular, for losses in $[0,1]$:

::: key
[Key result — Hoeffding for a loss in [0, 1]]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{P}\big(|\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| \geq \varepsilon\big) \leq 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.
$$
:::

::: proof
*Sketch in three moves.*

1.  **Hoeffding's lemma.** For centered $X \in [a,b]$, one bounds its generating function. By convexity of $u \mapsto e^{su}$, the curve lies below the chord joining $(a, e^{sa})$ and $(b, e^{sb})$, hence
    $$
    e^{sX} \leq \frac{b - X}{b - a}e^{sa} + \frac{X - a}{b - a}e^{sb}.
    $$
    Taking expectations,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] \leq \frac{b}{b-a}e^{sa} - \frac{a}{b-a}e^{sb} = e^{\varphi(s)},
    $$
    with $\varphi(0) = \varphi'(0) = 0$ and $\varphi''(s) \leq (b-a)^2/4$, so $\varphi(s) \leq s^2(b-a)^2/8$ (second-order Taylor remainder).
2.  **Multiplication.** For centered $S_n$, independence gives
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[e^{sS_n}] = \prod_i \mathbb{E}[e^{sX_i}] \leq \exp\big(s^2 \sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2/8\big).
    $$
3.  **Chernoff.** For all $s > 0$,
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(S_n \geq t) \leq e^{-st}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{sS_n}] \leq \exp\big(-st + \tfrac{s^2}{8}\sum_i(b_i - a_i)^2\big).
    $$
    The right-hand side is minimal at $s^\star = 4t/\sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2$, which gives $\exp(-2t^2/\sum_i (b_i-a_i)^2)$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why this is central in ML]{.tag} Hoeffding says: *for a fixed $f$*, $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f)$ is exponentially close to $\mathcal{R}(f)$. But the learner chooses $\hat f_n$ while *looking at the data* — one must then control $\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}$ over the whole class: this is precisely the subject of chapter 8 (uniform convergence, VC dimension, Rademacher complexity). Without this supplement, nothing can be proved about overfitting.
:::

### 0.2. Gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent {#gd-sgd}

The official description of the course announces "tools from optimization theory, and how to use them for machine learning". Almost every estimator of this module is the minimizer of an empirical risk $F(\theta) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\theta)$, where $\ell_i$ is the loss on example $i$. When no closed form exists (logistic regression, the lasso, boosting, neural networks), the minimizer is computed iteratively. Two numbers of the problem govern how fast this works: the smoothness constant and the curvature.

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Smoothness, strong convexity, condition number]{.tag} A differentiable function $f$ is **$L$-smooth** if its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz:
$$
\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \leq L\|x - y\|.
$$
It is **$\mu$-strongly convex** ($\mu > 0$) if $f - \frac{\mu}{2}\|\cdot\|^2$ is convex. For a twice-differentiable $f$, these mean $\mu I \preceq \nabla^2 f(x) \preceq L I$ for every $x$.

The ratio $\kappa = L/\mu \geq 1$ is the **condition number**: the larger it is, the more elongated the level sets and the slower gradient descent becomes.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Convergence of gradient descent]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth with a minimizer $x^\star$, and run $x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta\nabla f(x_t)$ with $\eta = 1/L$. Then

-   **(i)** (sublinear rate)
    $$
    f(x_t) - f(x^\star) \leq \dfrac{L\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{2t};
    $$
-   **(ii)** if moreover $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex (linear, also called geometric, rate),
    $$
    \|x_t - x^\star\|^2 \leq (1 - 1/\kappa)^t\,\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2.
    $$

::: proof
*Proof of (ii) for a quadratic $f(x) = \frac12 (x - x^\star)^\top A (x - x^\star)$ with $\mu I \preceq A \preceq LI$, the case met in least squares.* The gradient is $A(x - x^\star)$, so the error $e_t = x_t - x^\star$ satisfies $e_{t+1} = (I - \eta A)\,e_t$.

The eigenvalues of $I - A/L$ lie in $[0, 1 - \mu/L]$, hence $\|e_{t+1}\| \leq (1 - 1/\kappa)\|e_t\|$ and
$$
\|e_t\|^2 \leq (1 - 1/\kappa)^{2t}\|e_0\|^2 \leq (1-1/\kappa)^t\|e_0\|^2.
$$

The general statements (i) and (ii) follow from the descent lemma
$$
f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle\nabla f(x), y - x\rangle + \frac L2\|y - x\|^2
$$
combined with convexity (and, for (ii), strong convexity); see Garrigos & Gower (2023), section 3.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.6 — Step size on least squares]{.tag} For $F(\theta) = \frac{1}{2n}\|y - X\theta\|^2$, the Hessian is $H = X^\top X/n$, so $L$-smoothness and strong convexity hold with $L = \lambda_{\max}(H)$ and $\mu = \lambda_{\min}(H)$.

Take two centred, uncorrelated features with variances $4$ and $0.04$: $H = \mathrm{diag}(4, 0.04)$, so $L = 4$, $\mu = 0.04$ and $\kappa = 100$.

The recursion $e_{t+1} = (I - \eta H)e_t$ diverges as soon as $\eta > 2/L = 0.5$, because the factor $|1 - 4\eta|$ exceeds 1. With $\eta = 1/L = 0.25$, the first coordinate is solved in one step ($1 - 0.25 \times 4 = 0$).

But the second coordinate shrinks by only $1 - 0.01 = 0.99$ per step: about $\ln(100)/0.01 \approx 460$ iterations to divide its error by 100.

Standardizing both features to unit variance gives $\kappa = 1$ and convergence in one step. This is the optimization reason, beyond interpretability, for the `StandardScaler` placed in every pipeline of chapter 1.
:::

**Stochastic gradient descent (SGD).** One full gradient costs $\mathcal{O}(nd)$, which is prohibitive when $n$ reaches millions. SGD replaces it by the gradient of one example drawn uniformly at random, or of a mini-batch $B_t$ of size $b$:
$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta_t\,\frac1b\sum_{i \in B_t}\nabla \ell_i(\theta_t).
$$
Because $\mathbb{E}_i[\nabla \ell_i(\theta)] = \nabla F(\theta)$, the step is right *on average*; its variance decreases like $1/b$ when the mini-batch is drawn with replacement.

Two regimes follow. With a constant step, SGD reaches a neighbourhood of the minimizer whose size is proportional to $\eta$ times the gradient noise, and then oscillates there. With decreasing steps such that $\sum_t \eta_t = \infty$ and $\sum_t \eta_t^2 < \infty$ (for example $\eta_t \propto 1/t$), the iterates converge (Robbins–Monro conditions).

For a convex loss, if $\|\theta_0 - \theta^\star\| \leq R$ and the stochastic gradients satisfy $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla \ell_i(\theta_t)\|^2 \leq G^2$ along the iterates, the averaged iterate $\bar\theta_T$ obtained with $\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)$ satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}[F(\bar\theta_T)] - F(\theta^\star) \leq RG/\sqrt T.
$$
This rate is slower per iteration than theorem 0.5, but each iteration is $n/b$ times cheaper — the trade-off behind `partial_fit` in section 4.6 and behind the training of every neural network in the Deep Learning module.

::: note
[Non-smooth penalties: the proximal step]{.tag} The lasso objective $\frac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda\|\theta\|_1$ is not differentiable at zero, so plain gradient descent does not apply. The **proximal gradient** method (ISTA) takes a gradient step on the smooth part and then applies the soft thresholding of proposition 2.6 coordinate by coordinate:
$$
\theta \leftarrow S_{\eta\lambda}\big(\theta - \eta\,\tfrac2n X^\top(X\theta - y)\big),
$$
with $S_\tau(z) = \mathrm{sign}(z)(|z| - \tau)_+$. This is why the lasso solvers of scikit-learn produce exact zeros. With the orthogonal design of proposition 2.6, the smooth part is $2$-smooth, and one step of size $\eta = 1/2$ lands on the exact solution.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d = 10_000, 5
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); theta_star = rng.normal(size=d)
y = X @ theta_star + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=n)

L = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X / n).max()          # smoothness constant
theta = np.zeros(d)
for t in range(100):                                 # full gradient descent, step 1/L
    theta -= (1 / L) * X.T @ (X @ theta - y) / n

theta_sgd = np.zeros(d)
for t in range(1, 2001):                             # mini-batch SGD, b = 32, decreasing step
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=32)
    grad = X[idx].T @ (X[idx] @ theta_sgd - y[idx]) / 32
    theta_sgd -= 0.5 / np.sqrt(t) * grad
print(np.linalg.norm(theta - theta_star), np.linalg.norm(theta_sgd - theta_star))
```

### 0.3. Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence {#entropy-kl}

Classification losses, the EM algorithm of chapter 7 and the training objective of every language model compare two probability distributions. Three quantities do this job. We define them on a finite set; for densities, integrals replace the sums.

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Entropy, cross-entropy, Kullback–Leibler divergence]{.tag} For distributions $p$ and $q$ on a finite set $\mathcal{Z}$, with $q(z) > 0$ wherever $p(z) > 0$:
$$
H(p) = -\sum_z p(z)\log p(z), \qquad H(p, q) = -\sum_z p(z)\log q(z), \qquad \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_z p(z)\log\frac{p(z)}{q(z)}.
$$
The entropy $H(p)$ measures the uncertainty of $p$. The cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ is the average code length when data drawn from $p$ are coded with a code built for $q$, and the KL divergence is the excess length. With the natural logarithm they are measured in nats; with $\log_2$, in bits, as in the impurity of section 6.1.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Gibbs' inequality and maximum likelihood]{.tag}

-   **(i)** $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \geq 0$, with equality if and only if $p = q$.
-   **(ii)** The cross-entropy splits into entropy plus divergence:
    $$
    H(p, q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \geq H(p).
    $$
-   **(iii)** For a sample $z_1, \dots, z_n$ with empirical distribution $\hat p_n$ and a model $q_\theta$,
    $$
    -\frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \log q_\theta(z_i) = H(\hat p_n, q_\theta) = H(\hat p_n) + \mathrm{KL}(\hat p_n \,\|\, q_\theta).
    $$
    Since $H(\hat p_n)$ does not depend on $\theta$, maximizing the likelihood is minimizing the cross-entropy, and also the KL divergence from the data to the model.

::: proof
-   **(i)** The logarithm is strictly concave. Jensen's inequality under $p$, applied to the variable $q(Z)/p(Z)$, gives
    $$
    -\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\log\frac{q(Z)}{p(Z)}\Big] \leq \log \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\frac{q(Z)}{p(Z)}\Big] = \log \sum_{z :\, p(z) > 0} q(z) \leq \log 1 = 0.
    $$
    Equality in Jensen forces $q/p$ to be a constant $c$ on the support of $p$; equality in the last step forces $c = 1$, so $p = q$.
-   **(ii)** Write $\log(p/q) = \log p - \log q$ in the definition of KL.
-   **(iii)** Grouping equal values, the left-hand side is $-\sum_z \hat p_n(z) \log q_\theta(z)$; then apply (ii).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The logistic loss of proposition 3.2 is (iii) for the Bernoulli model of the label given $x$, and the softmax loss of language models is (iii) for the next token. The [Refresher in Statistics, section 9.3](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#likelihood-cross-entropy) derives (iii) for conditional models.

**Mutual information.** The dependence between two variables is the divergence between their joint law and the product of their marginals:
$$
I(X; Y) = \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{XY} \,\|\, p_X \otimes p_Y\big) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \geq 0,
$$
where $H(Y \mid X)$ is the average entropy of $Y$ once $X$ is known. By (i), it is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. It is the information gain of the trees of section 6.1 and one of the filter scores of section 4.7.

::: ex
[Example 0.9 — Forward and reverse KL on a bimodal target]{.tag} The target is the mixture
$$
p = \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(-3, 1) + \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(3, 1),
$$
and we fit one Gaussian $q = \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$. KL is not symmetric, and the two directions give different fits.

-   **Forward KL**, minimizing $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)$ as maximum likelihood does. The penalty is large wherever $p$ has mass and $q$ has none, so $q$ must cover both modes. The optimum matches the mean and the variance of $p$:
    $$
    m = 0, \qquad s^2 = 1 + 9 = 10.
    $$
-   **Reverse KL**, minimizing $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$ as the E-step of chapter 7 and variational inference do. The penalty is large wherever the fit puts mass and the target has little, so $q$ settles on one mode, near $\mathcal{N}(3, 1)$ or $\mathcal{N}(-3, 1)$, at a cost close to $\log 2$.

Forward KL is *mass-covering*; reverse KL is *mode-seeking*. A numerical minimization over $(m, s)$ confirms both fits.
:::

### 0.4. Lagrangian duality and KKT conditions (self-study) {#duality}

Read this section alone before session 3, where Exercise 2 first needs it. Many estimators minimize a function under constraints: the SVM of section 3.2 is solved through its dual, and Exercises 2 and 9 minimize under constraints. Duality turns each constraint into a price, and the KKT conditions characterize the optimum.

::: def
[Definition 0.10 — Lagrangian and dual problem]{.tag} Consider the problem
$$
p^\star = \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} f(x) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad g_i(x) \leq 0 \ (i \leq m), \qquad h_j(x) = 0 \ (j \leq r).
$$
Its **Lagrangian** attaches a multiplier $\alpha_i \geq 0$ to each inequality and $\nu_j \in \mathbb{R}$ to each equality:
$$
\mathcal{L}(x, \alpha, \nu) = f(x) + \sum_i \alpha_i g_i(x) + \sum_j \nu_j h_j(x).
$$
The **dual function** is $\psi(\alpha, \nu) = \inf_x \mathcal{L}(x, \alpha, \nu)$, and the **dual problem** is
$$
\psi^\star = \max_{\alpha \geq 0,\ \nu} \psi(\alpha, \nu).
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.11 — Weak duality, strong duality, KKT]{.tag}

-   **(i) Weak duality**: $\psi^\star \leq p^\star$ always.
-   **(ii) Strong duality (Slater)**: if $f$ and the $g_i$ are convex, the $h_j$ are affine, and some point satisfies every $g_i(x) < 0$ and every $h_j(x) = 0$, then $\psi^\star = p^\star$.
-   **(iii) KKT conditions**: under the assumptions of (ii), with $f$ and the $g_i$ differentiable, a feasible $x^\star$ is optimal if and only if there exist $\alpha^\star \geq 0$ and $\nu^\star$ with
    $$
    \nabla f(x^\star) + \sum_i \alpha_i^\star \nabla g_i(x^\star) + \sum_j \nu_j^\star \nabla h_j(x^\star) = 0 \quad \text{(stationarity)},
    $$
    and $\alpha_i^\star g_i(x^\star) = 0$ for every $i$ (complementary slackness).

::: proof
*Proof of (i).* Take a feasible $x$ and $\alpha \geq 0$. Each $\alpha_i g_i(x) \leq 0$ and each $h_j(x) = 0$, so
$$
\psi(\alpha, \nu) \leq \mathcal{L}(x, \alpha, \nu) \leq f(x).
$$
Take the supremum over $(\alpha, \nu)$ on the left and the infimum over feasible $x$ on the right.

The proof of (ii) separates two convex sets by a hyperplane (Boyd & Vandenberghe, 2004, section 5.3). In (iii), complementary slackness says that a multiplier can be positive only on an active constraint: this is how section 3.2 reads the support vectors.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.12 — The constraint of Exercise 2]{.tag} Minimize $\|a\|^2$ over $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$ under $\mathbf{1}^\top a = 1$. The Lagrangian is
$$
\mathcal{L}(a, \nu) = \|a\|^2 + \nu(\mathbf{1}^\top a - 1).
$$
Stationarity gives $2a + \nu\mathbf{1} = 0$, so every $a_i$ equals $-\nu/2$. The constraint then gives $\nu = -2/n$, hence
$$
a_i = 1/n \quad \text{for every } i,
$$
with optimal value $1/n$. The problem is convex with an affine constraint, so these conditions are sufficient.
:::

**Linear programs.** When the objective and the constraints are affine, the dual is again a linear program:
$$
\min_{x \geq 0} \ c^\top x \ \ \text{s.t.} \ \ Ax \geq b \qquad \text{has the dual} \qquad \max_{y \geq 0} \ b^\top y \ \ \text{s.t.} \ \ A^\top y \leq c.
$$
For linear programs, strong duality holds as soon as the primal has a finite optimum, with no Slater condition. Linear-programming duality comes back in reinforcement learning (the linear program of a Markov decision process) and in optimal transport.

## 1. The statistical framework of learning {#ch1}

Concrete scene: you fit a classifier on 60,000 digits (MNIST-like), train accuracy 99.8%, test 91%. The model "works"… and memorizes. Conversely, an under-regularized linear model may stall at 85% everywhere. This chapter names those gaps: risk vs empirical risk, bias-variance, validation. Theory comes after the symptom.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Tuning hyperparameters on the test set; ignoring class imbalance; believing a falling loss ⇒ generalization. All three sabotage a sklearn pipeline as much as an LLM fine-tune.
:::

::: note
[Learning paradigms and the pipeline]{.tag} Machine learning is usually divided by the kind of feedback the data provide. **Supervised learning** observes labelled pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ and learns a predictor $f(x) \approx y$: regression when $y$ is real, classification when $y$ is a class (chapters 1 to 6).

**Unsupervised learning** observes only the $x_i$ and looks for structure: groups (clustering), a low-dimensional representation (dimensionality reduction) or a density (chapter 7). **Self-supervised learning** manufactures labels from the data themselves, for example by hiding a word and predicting it; this is how language models are pretrained (Deep Learning module, section 6.5). **Reinforcement learning** has no labels at all: an agent chooses actions and receives scalar rewards (Deep Learning module, section 1.5).

Whatever the paradigm, a project follows the same **pipeline**: collect and split the data, learn the preprocessing on the training part only, fit and select models, evaluate once on held-out data, then inspect the errors. Chapter 4 makes each step precise.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — iid framework and risk]{.tag} One observes an iid sample $D_n = (X_i, Y_i)_{i \leq n}$ with law $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$. For a **loss** $\ell : \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}_+$, written $\ell(\hat y, y)$ with the prediction first, the **risk** of a predictor $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is
$$
\mathcal{R}(f) = \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(f(X), Y)\big],
$$
and the (observable) **empirical risk**:
$$
\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(X_i), Y_i).
$$
The **Bayes risk** is $\mathcal{R}^\star = \inf_f \mathcal{R}(f)$, the infimum over all measurable functions.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Empirical risk minimization (ERM)]{.tag} Given a model class $\mathcal{F}$, learning solves
$$
\hat f_n \in \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \ \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f).
$$
All of ML consists in choosing $\mathcal{F}$ (linear? tree-based? network?), $\ell$ (quadratic, logistic, hinge...), and in controlling the gap
$$
\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f).
$$
:::

The excess risk decomposes into two contributions of different natures:

::: key
[Key result — approximation and estimation errors]{.tag}
$$
\underbrace{\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \mathcal{R}^\star}_{\text{excess risk}} = \underbrace{\inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) - \mathcal{R}^\star}_{\text{approximation error}} + \underbrace{\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)}_{\text{estimation error}}.
$$
:::

The first depends only on the choice of $\mathcal{F}$ (modeling bias), the second on the sample and the size of $\mathcal{F}$ (variance, chapter 8). Enlarging $\mathcal{F}$ decreases the first and increases the second: the whole dilemma is there.

### 1.1. Bias-variance

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Bias-variance decomposition (quadratic loss)]{.tag} Assume $Y = f^\star(X) + \varepsilon$ with $f^\star(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$ and noise $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2$. For an estimator $\hat f_n$ built on $D_n$ independent of the test pair $(X, Y)$:

::: key
[Key result — bias-variance decomposition]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(Y - \hat f_n(X))^2\big] = \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}} + \mathbb{E}\big[\underbrace{\text{bias}^2(\hat f_n)}_{\text{underfitting}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\hat f_n)}_{\text{overfitting}}\big].
$$
:::

::: proof
Condition on $X = x$ and on $D_n$ (the total expectation is then taken over both).

On the one hand $\hat f_n(x)$ depends only on $D_n$, and $Y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon$ with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x, D_n] = 0$; the cross term therefore vanishes:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(Y - \hat f_n(x))^2\big] = \sigma^2 + \mathbb{E}\big[(f^\star(x) - \hat f_n(x))^2\big].
$$

On the other hand, for any variable $Z$, $\mathbb{E}[Z^2] = (\mathbb{E}Z)^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z)$ applied to $Z = f^\star(x) - \hat f_n(x)$ (the variance is over the randomness of $D_n$):
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(f^\star(x) - \hat f_n(x))^2\big] = \big(f^\star(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f_n(x)]\big)^2 + \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f_n(x)\big).
$$

Finally integrate over $x \sim \mathbb{P}_X$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A class $\mathcal{F}$ that is too small ⇒ high bias; too large ⇒ high variance. This decomposition is *diagnostic*: high training and test errors ⇒ underfitting (enlarge the model); low training and high test ⇒ overfitting (regularize, more data, chapters 2 and 8). No algorithm is universally better (the "no free lunch" theorem): prior knowledge about the data matters as much as the algorithm.

### 1.2. Cross-validation

The risk $\mathcal{R}$ is unobservable: it is estimated by setting data aside. **k-fold**: split into $k$ blocks, train $k$ times while rotating the test block, average.

*Leave-one-out* ($k = n$) has low bias but high estimation variance and costs $n$ trainings; $k = 5$ or $10$ is the standard compromise.

Program rules: never fit preprocessing on the test set; a final *test* set that is looked at only once; *validation* serves to choose hyperparameters and models (chapter 4 for the nested version).

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.0))
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(-scores.mean(), scores.std())
```

## 2. Linear regression and regularization {#ch2}

### 2.1. Ordinary least squares

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Gaussian linear model]{.tag} One observes $y = X\theta + \varepsilon$ where $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ is fixed (the design), $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^p$, and one assumes:

-   (H1) $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$;
-   (H2) $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I_n$ (homoscedasticity);
-   (H3) independent components;
-   (H4, optional) $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$.

The least squares estimator minimizes
$$
\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\theta) = \tfrac1n \|y - X\theta\|^2.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Normal equations]{.tag} If $X^\top X$ is invertible, the unique minimizer is $$\hat\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y.$$

::: proof
Expand
$$
\|y - X\theta\|^2 = \theta^\top X^\top X\,\theta - 2\,\theta^\top X^\top y + \|y\|^2.
$$
The gradient in $\theta$ is $2X^\top X \theta - 2X^\top y$ (symmetric matrix for the quadratic term); setting it to zero gives the *normal equations*
$$
X^\top X\theta = X^\top y.
$$
The Hessian $2X^\top X \succeq 0$ is positive definite as soon as $\mathrm{rank}(X) = p$: the function is strictly convex, the stationary point is the unique global minimum.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Geometry: an orthogonal projection]{.tag} $\hat y = X\hat\theta = P y$ with
$$
P = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top
$$
the orthogonal projection onto $\mathrm{Im}(X)$. One checks $P^2 = P = P^\top$; the residual $e = y - \hat y$ satisfies $X^\top e = 0$, i.e. $e \perp \mathrm{Im}(X)$.

The $h_{ii} = P_{ii}$ (the *leverages*) measure the influence of each observation, with $\sum_i h_{ii} = p$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Gauss-Markov]{.tag} Under (H1)-(H3), for every $c \in \mathbb{R}^p$, the estimator $c^\top\hat\theta$ is the *best linear unbiased estimator* (BLUE) of $c^\top\theta$: among the $a^\top y$ with $\mathbb{E}[a^\top y] = c^\top\theta$ for every $\theta$, it has minimal variance.

::: proof
A linear estimator $a^\top y$ is unbiased for every $\theta$ iff $a^\top X = c^\top$. Set $a_\star = X(X^\top X)^{-1}c \in \mathrm{Im}(X)$: $a_\star^\top X = c^\top$, so $a_\star$ is admissible, and
$$
\mathrm{Var}(a_\star^\top y) = \sigma^2 \|a_\star\|^2 = \sigma^2 c^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}c,
$$
which is indeed the variance of $c^\top\hat\theta$.

Let $a$ be any admissible vector and $h = a - a_\star$; then $h^\top X = 0$, so $h \perp \mathrm{Im}(X) \ni a_\star$, hence
$$
\mathrm{Var}(a^\top y) = \sigma^2\|a\|^2 = \sigma^2\big(\|a_\star\|^2 + \|h\|^2\big) \geq \sigma^2\|a_\star\|^2 = \mathrm{Var}(c^\top\hat\theta),
$$
with equality iff $a = a_\star$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Inference: confidence intervals (under H4)]{.tag} Under Gaussian noise (a linear variable of a Gaussian vector),
$$
\hat\theta \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\theta,\ \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\big),
$$
and $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac{1}{n-p}\|y - X\hat\theta\|^2$ is an unbiased estimator independent of $\hat\theta$.

Writing $v_j = [(X^\top X)^{-1}]_{jj}$, the statistic $(\hat\theta_j - \theta_j)/(\hat\sigma\sqrt{v_j})$ follows a Student distribution with $n - p$ degrees of freedom, giving the 95% confidence interval:
$$
\hat\theta_j \pm t_{0.975}^{\,n-p}\; \hat\sigma \sqrt{v_j}.
$$
(Reminder on usual distributions: cf. Refresher Statistics module.) The (estimator, standard deviation) pair reported by any serious regressor is read here: a coefficient whose interval contains $0$ is not "significant".
:::

::: ex
[Residual analysis — the model's quality control]{.tag} The assumptions (H1)-(H4) are checked graphically on the residuals $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$ (standardized $r_i = e_i/\big(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}\big)$):

-   residuals *vs* fitted values (a curvature betrays a missing nonlinearity; a funnel, heteroscedasticity — think of transforming $y$ or weighting);
-   Gaussian quantile-quantile plot (departure of the noise from normality);
-   spotting high-leverage points $h_{ii} \gg 2p/n$ that "pull" the line.
:::

### 2.2. Regularization: ridge and lasso

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Ridge and lasso]{.tag} $$\hat\theta_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\theta \Big\{\tfrac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|_2^2\Big\} = (X^\top X + n\lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y,$$ $$\hat\theta_{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\theta \Big\{\tfrac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|_1\Big\}.$$ Ridge shrinks all coefficients (a solution always exists); the lasso produces coefficients that are *exactly zero* (variable selection).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Ridge: spectral effect]{.tag} Write the SVD $X = U\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_j)\,V^\top$. Then
$$
\hat\theta_{\text{ridge}} = \sum_j \frac{\sigma_j\, u_j^\top y}{\sigma_j^2 + n\lambda}\; v_j, \qquad\text{whereas}\qquad \hat\theta = \sum_j \frac{u_j^\top y}{\sigma_j}\;v_j.
$$
Ridge damps each direction $v_j$ by the factor $\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2 + n\lambda)$: the well-explained directions (large $\sigma_j$) pass through, the ill-conditioned directions (collinearities, $\sigma_j \to 0$) are crushed — exactly the ones that made the least squares variance explode.

In particular $\|\hat\theta_{\text{ridge}}\|$ decreases from $\|\hat\theta\|$ toward $0$ as $\lambda$ grows.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — Lasso with an orthogonal design: soft thresholding]{.tag} Assume the columns of $X$ are orthogonal with squared norm $n$ (uncorrelated standardized features), that is $X^\top X = n I_p$, and set $z = X^\top y/n$. Then the lasso of definition 2.4 is
$$
\hat\theta_{\text{lasso},j} = \mathrm{sign}(z_j)\,\big(|z_j| - \lambda/2\big)_+.
$$
With orthonormal columns ($X^\top X = I_p$) instead, the same computation thresholds $X^\top y$ at $n\lambda/2$.

::: proof
Expanding the square with $X^\top X = nI_p$ gives
$$
\tfrac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 = \|\theta - z\|^2 + \text{const.},
$$
so the lasso objective is twice a functional that separates over the coordinates:
$$
\sum_j \big\{\tfrac12(z_j - \theta_j)^2 + \tfrac{\lambda}{2}|\theta_j|\big\}.
$$
For $z_j > 0$, the optimum is either $\theta_j = 0$ (cost $z_j^2/2$), or a stationary point in the region $\theta_j > 0$ where the norm-1 term is differentiable:
$$
z_j - \theta_j = \lambda/2,
$$
of cost $\lambda z_j/2 - \lambda^2/8 < z_j^2/2$ as soon as $z_j > \lambda/2$. Hence the thresholding; the case $z_j < 0$ is symmetric.[∎]{.qed}
:::

It is this "dead zone" around zero that sets coefficients *exactly* to zero: in arbitrary dimension, the path $\lambda \mapsto \hat\theta_{\text{lasso}}(\lambda)$ is *piecewise linear* (the LARS algorithm of Efron et al., 2004), which `lasso_path` visualizes.
::::

::: note
[Geometry of regularization]{.tag} Constraint $\|\theta\|_1 \leq t$ = diamond: the corners on the axes explain the sparsity; $\|\theta\|_2 \leq t$ = ball: isotropic shrinkage. Regularization is the first weapon against variance — and the ancestor of the *weight decay* of neural networks ($\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2$ added to the loss in the Deep Learning module).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Bayesian reading: ridge = Gaussian prior, lasso = Laplacian prior]{.tag} Assume $y = X\theta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$.

-   **(i)** If $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 I)$, the MAP (maximum a posteriori) is exactly $\hat\theta_{\text{ridge}}$ with $\lambda = \sigma^2/(n\tau^2)$.
-   **(ii)** If the coordinates of $\theta$ are iid with Laplacian density $p(\theta_j) = \tfrac{1}{2b}e^{-|\theta_j|/b}$, the MAP is $\hat\theta_{\text{lasso}}$ with $\lambda = 2\sigma^2/(nb)$.

::: proof
By Bayes' formula,
$$
-\log p(\theta \mid y) = \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - X\theta\|^2 - \sum_j \log p(\theta_j) + \text{const.}
$$

-   **(i)**
    $$
    -\log p(\theta_j) = \theta_j^2/(2\tau^2) + \text{const.}:
    $$
    minimizing amounts to minimizing
    $$
    \|y - X\theta\|^2 + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\|\theta\|_2^2.
    $$
-   **(ii)**
    $$
    -\log p(\theta_j) = |\theta_j|/b + \text{const.}:
    $$
    minimize
    $$
    \|y - X\theta\|^2 + \tfrac{2\sigma^2}{b}\|\theta\|_1.
    $$

In both cases the negative log-posterior was multiplied by $2\sigma^2$. Dividing by $n$ gives the objectives of definition 2.4, with $\lambda = \sigma^2/(n\tau^2)$ for ridge and $\lambda = 2\sigma^2/(nb)$ for the lasso.[∎]{.qed}
:::

Moral: regularizing = encoding a prior (small / sparse coefficients); the Laplacian prior, peaked at zero, "pushes" coefficients toward zero more strongly than the Gaussian.
::::

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, lasso_path
for lam in [1e-4, 1e-2, 1.0, 10.0]:
    l = Lasso(alpha=lam).fit(X, y)
    print(f"lambda={lam:8.3f}  nonzero coeffs = {(l.coef_ != 0).sum()}")

# lasso regularization path (piecewise linear, cf. LARS)
alphas, coefs, _ = lasso_path(X, y, alphas=np.logspace(-3, 1, 100))
```

## 3. Classification: logistic regression and SVM {#ch3}

### 3.1. Logistic regression

::: def
[Definition 3.1]{.tag} For $Y \in \{0, 1\}$, one directly models $$\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid X = x) = \sigma(\langle \theta, x\rangle) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\langle \theta, x\rangle}},$$ where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. The log-odds is linear: $\log \tfrac{p}{1-p} = \langle\theta, x\rangle$ — hence an interpretable reading of the coefficients (odds ratio $\approx e^{\theta_j}$ for $x_j$ increased by one unit).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Likelihood and cross-entropy]{.tag} Maximizing the likelihood
$$
\prod_i \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)^{y_i}(1 - \sigma(\theta^\top x_i))^{1 - y_i}
$$
is equivalent to minimizing the **cross-entropy**
$$
\hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta \ \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \log\!\big(1 + e^{-y'_i \langle\theta, x_i\rangle}\big), \qquad y'_i \in \{-1, +1\}.
$$

::: proof
$-\log$-likelihood = $\sum_i -y_i\log p_i - (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i)$ with $p_i = \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)$. Writing $y'_i = 2y_i - 1$, one checks
$$
-y_i \log p_i - (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i) = \log(1 + e^{-y'_i \theta^\top x_i}):
$$
for $y_i = 1$, $1 - p_i = \sigma(-\theta^\top x_i)$ and $1/(1-p_i) = 1 + e^{\theta^\top x_i}$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Convexity, gradient, Hessian]{.tag} Set $p_i(\theta) = \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)$ and
$$
F(\theta) = \tfrac1n\sum_i \log(1 + e^{-y'_i\theta^\top x_i}).
$$
Then:

-   **(i)** $F$ is convex, and strictly convex if $\ker X = \{0\}$;
-   **(ii)** $\nabla F(\theta) = \tfrac1n X^\top(p(\theta) - y)$;
-   **(iii)** with $w_i = p_i(1 - p_i) \in \,]0, 1/4]$,
    $$
    \nabla^2 F(\theta) = \tfrac1n X^\top \mathrm{diag}\big(w_i(\theta)\big) X.
    $$

::: proof
-   **(i)** Let $g(z) = \log(1 + e^{-z})$. Then $g'(z) = \tfrac{-e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}} = -\sigma(-z)$ and
    $$
    g''(z) = \sigma(-z)\big(1 - \sigma(-z)\big) = \frac{e^{-z}}{(1 + e^{-z})^2} > 0,
    $$
    (the rate of change of $\sigma'$ — or direct differentiation of $\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)$). Hence $g$ is convex; each $g(\pm\theta^\top x_i)$ is convex in $\theta$ (composition with an affine map), and $F$, a sum, is convex.
-   **(ii)** The loss of example $i$ is $g(y'_i\theta^\top x_i)$. By the chain rule with $g'$ above,
    $$
    \nabla_\theta\, g(y'_i\theta^\top x_i) = g'(y'_i\theta^\top x_i)\, y'_i x_i = -y'_i x_i\, \sigma(-y'_i \theta^\top x_i).
    $$
    If $y_i = 1$, then $y'_i\sigma(-y'_i\theta^\top x_i) = 1 - p_i$; if $y_i = 0$, it equals $-\sigma(\theta^\top x_i) = -p_i$. In both cases it is $y_i - p_i$, so each example contributes $x_i(p_i - y_i)$, and averaging gives (ii).
-   **(iii)** The Jacobian of $p(\theta)$ is $\mathrm{diag}(w_i)X$ (since $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$), giving the announced Hessian. It is a weighted Gram matrix, not a multiple of $X^\top X$: for every $v$,
    $$
    v^\top X^\top \mathrm{diag}(w_i) X v = \sum_i w_i\,(x_i^\top v)^2 \geq 0,
    $$
    because every $w_i > 0$, with equality only if $Xv = 0$. The Hessian is therefore positive semidefinite, and positive definite when the columns of $X$ are independent.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Practical consequences]{.tag} Convex + smooth ⇒ a unique global optimum, reached by gradient descent or Newton. The Newton method here reads $\theta \leftarrow \theta + (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top(y - p)$: this is exactly the iteratively reweighted regression (IRLS) well known from GLMs. This is *the* classification loss of neural networks (Deep Learning module) and of LLMs (softmax output = multiclass generalization $\log\sum_k e^{s_k} - s_{y}$).
:::

### 3.2. Margin SVM

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — SVM (soft margin, primal)]{.tag} $$\min_{\theta, b, \xi} \ \tfrac12 \|\theta\|^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y'_i(\langle\theta, x_i\rangle + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i, \quad \xi_i \geq 0.$$ Maximize the margin $\gamma = 1/\|\theta\|$ while tolerating the violations $\xi_i$ (soft constraints, $C$ = unit penalty). The classifier is $x \mapsto \mathrm{sign}(\langle\theta, x\rangle + b)$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — Dual of the SVM]{.tag} The primal above has the same solution as the dual problem $$\max_{\alpha} \ \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i - \frac12 \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i\alpha_j y'_i y'_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle \quad \text{s.t.} \quad 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C, \ \sum_i \alpha_i y'_i = 0,$$ and the primal solution is reconstructed via $\theta = \sum_i \alpha_i y'_i x_i$.

::: proof
**Lagrangian.** Associate a multiplier $\alpha_i \geq 0$ with each margin constraint and $\mu_i \geq 0$ with $\xi_i \geq 0$:
$$
\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\|\theta\|^2 + C\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i - \sum_i \alpha_i\big[y'_i(\theta^\top x_i + b) - 1 + \xi_i\big] - \sum_i \mu_i \xi_i.
$$

**Stationary conditions (KKT).**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\partial_\theta \mathcal{L} = 0 &\Rightarrow \theta = \sum_i \alpha_i y'_i x_i, \\
\partial_b \mathcal{L} = 0 &\Rightarrow \sum_i \alpha_i y'_i = 0, \\
\partial_{\xi_i} \mathcal{L} = 0 &\Rightarrow C = \alpha_i + \mu_i, \text{ i.e. } \alpha_i \leq C.
\end{aligned}
$$
The first condition says that the predictor is a combination of the data!

Substitute back: the term $\theta^\top\theta$ against $-\sum\alpha_i y'_i\theta^\top x_i$ gives $-\tfrac12\|\theta\|^2$, then replacing $\|\theta\|^2$ by the double sum.

The $\xi_i$ disappear exactly ($(C - \alpha_i - \mu_i)\xi_i = 0$); what remains is the announced dual function with $0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C$.

The primal is convex with affine constraints: Slater (strictly feasible, $C$ large enough or $\xi$ large enough) guarantees strong duality — dual optimum = primal optimum, and the KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Reading the complementarity conditions — who are the support vectors?]{.tag} The KKT complementarity conditions $\alpha_i\,[y'_i(\theta^\top x_i + b) - 1 + \xi_i] = 0$ and $(C - \alpha_i)\,\xi_i = 0$ sort the points into three families:

| Case | Position of the point | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $\alpha_i = 0$ | outside the margin band, well classified | none — any data point |
| $0 < \alpha_i < C$ | exactly *on* the margin $(\xi_i = 0)$ | "free" support vector |
| $\alpha_i = C$ | inside the band or misclassified $(\xi_i > 0)$ | "paying" support vector |

The solution depends *only* on the points with $\alpha_i > 0$ (dual sparsity): this is the robustness of SVMs to distant data, and the $\mathcal{O}(n_{\text{supp}})$ prediction cost. The constant $b$ is recovered from any point on the margin: $b = y'_i - \theta^\top x_i$.
:::

::: prop
[Theorem 3.6 — Margin generalization bounds (sketch)]{.tag} Let
$$
\mathcal{F}_R = \{x \mapsto \langle\theta, x\rangle : \|\theta\| \leq R,\ \|x\| \leq 1\}.
$$
Its Rademacher complexity (definition in chapter 8) satisfies $\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{F}_R) \leq R/\sqrt{n}$, independently of the dimension of $\mathcal{X}$. It follows, with high probability, for any score function with margin $\gamma$ (losses dominated by the hinge):
$$
\mathcal{R}(f) \ \leq\ \hat{\mathcal{R}}_{n,\gamma}(f) + \frac{2R}{\gamma\sqrt{n}} + \sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
*Sketch.*

-   **(i)** The hinge $(1 - t)_+$ is 1-Lipschitz: the contraction lemma brings the loss back to the score.
-   **(ii)** For the class of bounded scores,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}_\sigma \sup_{\|\theta\| \leq R} \tfrac1n\theta^\top\sum_i \sigma_i x_i = \tfrac{R}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_\sigma\big\|\sum_i \sigma_i x_i\big\| \leq \tfrac{R}{n}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\big\|\sum_i\sigma_ix_i\big\|^2} = \tfrac{R}{n}\sqrt{n} = \tfrac{R}{\sqrt n}
    $$
    (Cauchy-Schwarz, then orthogonality of the $\sigma_ix_i$ and $\|x_i\| \leq 1$).[∎]{.qed}

This "margin, not dimension" viewpoint watches over overfitting; it is developed in chapter 8, and further in the [Statistical Learning Theory](../m1p1-statistical-learning-theory/index.html) notes, kept for reference (that course is not in the LLGA list).
:::

### 3.3. Generative versus discriminative classifiers: naive Bayes {#naive-bayes}

Logistic regression models $\mathbb{P}(Y \mid X)$ directly, and the SVM only a decision boundary: both are **discriminative**. A **generative** classifier takes the opposite route: it models how each class produces its inputs, $p(x \mid y)$, together with the class proportions $\pi_y = \mathbb{P}(Y = y)$, and classifies with Bayes' formula.

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Generative classifier and naive Bayes]{.tag} A generative classifier predicts $\hat y(x) = \arg\max_k \ \pi_k\, p(x \mid Y = k)$, which is the Bayes classifier when the model is correct. **Naive Bayes** assumes that the features are independent *given the class*: $$p(x \mid Y = k) = \prod_{j=1}^d p_j(x_j \mid Y = k).$$ Each one-dimensional factor is estimated separately by maximum likelihood: Bernoulli frequencies for binary features (word present or absent), multinomial frequencies for counts, a per-class mean and variance for real features (Gaussian naive Bayes). The number of parameters grows linearly in $d$, and training is a single counting pass over the data.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.8 — Gaussian naive Bayes has a logistic posterior]{.tag} With two classes, $x_j \mid Y = k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{kj}, \sigma_j^2)$ (variances shared by the classes), $$\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(\theta^\top x + b), \qquad \theta_j = \frac{\mu_{1j} - \mu_{0j}}{\sigma_j^2}, \qquad b = \log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0} + \sum_j \frac{\mu_{0j}^2 - \mu_{1j}^2}{2\sigma_j^2}.$$

::: proof
By Bayes' formula,
$$
\log\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid x)} = \log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0} + \sum_j \log\frac{p_j(x_j \mid 1)}{p_j(x_j \mid 0)}.
$$
For each $j$, the Gaussian normalizing constants cancel and
$$
\frac{(x_j - \mu_{0j})^2 - (x_j - \mu_{1j})^2}{2\sigma_j^2} = \frac{(\mu_{1j} - \mu_{0j})\,x_j}{\sigma_j^2} + \frac{\mu_{0j}^2 - \mu_{1j}^2}{2\sigma_j^2}.
$$
The log-odds is therefore affine in $x$, and inverting $\log\frac{p}{1-p} = z$ gives $p = \sigma(z)$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The model family is the same as in section 3.1; only the fitting differs. Naive Bayes fits $\theta$ through the joint likelihood of $(x, y)$, which is efficient when its assumptions hold; logistic regression fits $\mathbb{P}(Y \mid x)$ only and remains consistent for that family when they fail.

Ng and Jordan (2002) made the trade-off precise: the generative classifier approaches its asymptotic error with a number of examples of order $\log d$, the discriminative one with order $d$, but the discriminative asymptotic error is never worse. Naive Bayes is therefore a strong baseline for small samples and high-dimensional text, and logistic regression usually wins once data are plentiful.

::: ex
[Example 3.9 — A two-word spam filter]{.tag} A training set has 40 spam and 60 legitimate emails. The word "free" appears in 24 spam and 6 legitimate emails; the word "meeting" appears in 4 spam and 30 legitimate emails.

For a new email containing "free" but not "meeting", the Bernoulli naive Bayes scores are
$$
\text{spam: } 0.4 \times \tfrac{24}{40} \times \big(1 - \tfrac{4}{40}\big) = 0.216, \qquad \text{legitimate: } 0.6 \times \tfrac{6}{60} \times \big(1 - \tfrac{30}{60}\big) = 0.03,
$$
so
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{spam} \mid x) = 0.216 / (0.216 + 0.03) \approx 0.88.
$$

Had "free" never occurred in a legitimate email, its estimated probability there would be $0$ and this single word would veto the class whatever the rest of the email says. **Laplace smoothing** replaces each frequency $m/n_k$ by $(m + 1)/(n_k + 2)$, which keeps every probability positive.
:::

## 4. Evaluation, big data and pipelines {#ch4}

### 4.1. Choosing your metric

| Metric | Definition | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| accuracy | $\frac{TP+TN}{n}$ | balanced classes |
| balanced accuracy | mean of per-class recall | mild imbalance |
| precision / recall | $\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$ / $\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$ | imbalance (fraud, spam) |
| F1 | harmonic mean of precision/recall | precision/recall trade-off |
| AUC-ROC | area under the ROC curve | ordering examples (ranking) |
| PR-AUC | area in precision-recall | very strong imbalance (more informative than ROC) |
| Brier | $\frac1n\sum_i (\hat p_i - y_i)^2$ | *calibrated* quality of probabilities |
| RMSE / MAE | squared / absolute errors | regression |

### 4.2. Nested cross-validation

Selecting a model *and* estimating its risk on the same folds is a well-documented optimism bias: the retained score is that of a "champion" chosen *among* the candidates on those same data — the exact mechanism of selection overfitting (chapter 8!). **Nested cross-validation** separates the two roles: the *inner* loop (on $k-1$ folds) chooses the hyperparameters, the *outer* loop (the remaining fold) evaluates the model thus chosen. Cost: $k_{\text{int}} \times k_{\text{ext}}$ trainings — the price of statistical honesty.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}, cv=5)
outer_scores = cross_val_score(grid, X, y, cv=10)   # outer loop: honest estimation
print(outer_scores.mean(), outer_scores.std())
```

### 4.3. Data leakage

::: note
[The four classic leaks — and the antidote]{.tag}

-   **(1)** Standardizing/imputing *before* the split: the test statistics contaminate the training.
-   **(2)** Target encoding (*target encoding*) computed on the whole set: the answer leaks into the features.
-   **(3)** Duplicates of the same entity (patient, sensor) split across both train and test: one evaluates memory, not generalization.
-   **(4)** Variables *posterior* to the predicted event (reimbursement amount to predict a default).

The antidote fits in one rule: *every transformation that "learns" lives inside the pipeline*, hence re-estimated on each training fold — this is exactly what scikit-learn's `Pipeline` and `ColumnTransformer` do, including for nested validators.
:::

```python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols),
])
model = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("clf", HistGradientBoostingClassifier())])
# model.fit on the train only; nothing is learned outside fit().
```

### 4.4. Imbalanced classes

With 0.5% of fraud, the trivial classifier "everything is normal" reaches 99.5% accuracy. Three levers:

-   **(i) the loss** — weight the classes via `class_weight="balanced"`: the $\propto 1/n_k$ weighting restores the balance in ERM;
-   **(ii) resampling** — oversampling the minority (SMOTE: interpolate between minority neighbors) or undersampling the majority, *always inside the training pipeline only* (otherwise: leakage);
-   **(iii) evaluation** — precision/recall, PR-AUC; and the decision threshold chosen *after* calibration (4.5), not at 0.5 by default.

### 4.5. Probability calibration

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Calibration]{.tag} A probability predictor $\hat p$ is *calibrated* if, among the cases where it announces $p$, the observed frequency of the event equals $p$:
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X) = p) = p.
$$
The *reliability diagram* (observed frequency *vs* predicted probability, per bin) and the Brier score $\frac1n\sum_i(\hat p_i - y_i)^2$ (a squared loss! cf. chapter 2) measure it.
:::

Two standard post-processings, learned on a separate calibration set: **Platt scaling** — fit a logistic regression (chapter 3) on the noisy score: $\hat p = \sigma(a\,s(x) + b)$; **isotonic regression** — the nonparametric monotone function closest to the reliability bins (more flexible, more data needed).

Caution: *discrimination and calibration are two distinct properties* — a model may excellently order examples (high AUC) while announcing systematically overconfident probabilities. SVM scores are not probabilities: going through calibration is indispensable as soon as one wants probabilities (cost/benefit decisions, stacking).

```python
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(estimator=svc, method="isotonic", cv=5).fit(X_train, y_train)
# check: sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve + Brier score
```

### 4.6. Big data: what does size change?

When $n$ explodes, theory plays *for* you (bounds in $\sqrt{d/n}$, chapter 8) but computation costs become the limiting factor. Switch to *incremental* methods (`partial_fit`/SGD: the stochastic gradient descent of [section 0.2](#gd-sgd), one pass at a time), to *hashing* for sparse text features, to histogram implementations (HistGradientBoosting), and to the stream methods of chapter 9 (River) when the data do not fit in memory.

Golden rule of the program: *a complete reference pipeline* — train/val/test split → preprocessing learned on train only → nested selection → single evaluation on test → error inspection (confusion matrix, residuals of chapter 2, subgroups) — to be replicated in all the labs and the running project. The [Year 1 end-of-year projects](../../projects/index.html#year1) use this pipeline as their [shared evaluation kit](../../projects/index.html#kit), completed by subgroup metrics (4.8), honest model comparison (4.9) and the paired, group-level comparison of the [Refresher in Statistics exit checkpoint](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#exit).

### 4.7. Feature selection {#feature-selection}

Removing useless features reduces variance, cost and the effort of interpretation. Three families of methods exist, and all three are *learning steps*: they must be fitted on training data only.

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Filter, wrapper and embedded selection]{.tag} A **filter** ranks features by a univariate score computed against the label (correlation, ANOVA $F$ statistic, mutual information, $\chi^2$) and keeps the top $k$; it is fast but blind to interactions: with $y = x_1 \oplus x_2$ (exclusive or), each feature alone carries no information although the pair determines $y$.

A **wrapper** searches over subsets using the validation error of the model itself; forward stepwise selection adds, at each step, the feature that most reduces that error, at a cost of about $kd$ model fits for $k$ features.

**Embedded** methods select while fitting: the lasso sets coefficients exactly to zero (section 2.2), and trees and forests rank features by importance (chapter 6); importances should be measured by permutation on held-out data, since impurity-based importances favour features with many distinct values.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — The selection-bias trap]{.tag} Take $n = 50$ samples, $d = 5000$ features of pure noise and random balanced labels: the true error of any classifier is 50%. Yet among 5000 noise features, the largest absolute sample correlation with the labels is of order $\sqrt{2\ln(2d)/n} \approx 0.6$, so a filter applied to all 50 samples finds features that look strongly predictive.

Cross-validating a classifier on those features *after* the selection is then badly optimistic: with 100 selected features and a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier, Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (*Elements of Statistical Learning*, section 7.10.2) report an average cross-validated error of 3%. The selection saw the test folds.

The correct procedure puts the selection inside the pipeline, so that it is refitted on the training part of each fold; the cross-validated error then returns to about 50%.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(50, 5000)); y = rng.permutation(np.repeat([0, 1], 25))  # pure noise
top = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(X, y).get_support()       # WRONG: selection on all data
print(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X[:, top], y, cv=5).mean())   # optimistic
pipe = make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20), LogisticRegression())  # RIGHT: inside the folds
print(cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5).mean())                            # close to 0.5
```

### 4.8. Subgroup evaluation and group fairness {#fairness}

An average score can hide a group on which the model fails. Before deployment, the error inspection of the reference pipeline (4.6) is repeated *per group*: by sex, age band, region, device, or any attribute on which errors would be costly or unfair.

The per-group metrics are computed on the held-out predictions of the pipeline, never on the training data. Each comes with its group size: a 20-point gap on a group of 30 people is mostly noise (section 4.9 gives the intervals).

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Three group-fairness criteria]{.tag} Let $A$ be a group attribute, $Y \in \{0, 1\}$ the label, $S \in [0, 1]$ a score and $\hat Y$ the decision. For all groups $a$ and $b$:

-   **demographic parity** asks for the same rate of positive decisions,
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = a) = \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = b);
    $$
-   **equalized odds** (Hardt, Price and Srebro, 2016) asks for the same true-positive and false-positive rates, that is, for $y \in \{0, 1\}$,
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid Y = y, A = a) = \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid Y = y, A = b);
    $$
    *equal opportunity* asks this for $y = 1$ only;
-   **calibration within groups** asks that definition 4.1 hold inside each group,
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid S = s, A = a) = s \quad \text{for every } a \text{ and } s.
    $$
:::

These criteria cannot all hold at once. The identity below, a simple count, shows why.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Precision, error rates and prevalence (Chouldechova, 2017)]{.tag} In a group with prevalence $\pi = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1)$, every decision rule satisfies
$$
\mathrm{FPR} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\cdot\frac{1 - \mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\cdot(1 - \mathrm{FNR}),
$$
where PPV is the precision, FPR the false-positive rate and FNR the false-negative rate. Hence, if two groups have different prevalences, a rule with the same precision in both (*predictive parity*) and the same false-negative rate has different false-positive rates, unless it makes no false positive at all.

Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017) prove the analogue for scores: calibration within groups and balanced error rates are incompatible, except for a perfect predictor or equal prevalences.

::: proof
Let $N_+$ and $N_-$ be the numbers of positives and negatives of the group, so $N_-/N_+ = (1 - \pi)/\pi$. By the definitions of the false-negative rate and of the precision,
$$
\mathrm{TP} = (1 - \mathrm{FNR})\,N_+, \qquad \mathrm{FP} = \mathrm{TP}\,\frac{1 - \mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}.
$$
Dividing $\mathrm{FP}$ by $N_-$ gives the identity.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.6 — Same precision, different false alarms]{.tag} Group $a$ has prevalence 0.5 and group $b$ has prevalence 0.2. A rule has precision 0.8 and false-negative rate 0.2 in both groups. By proposition 4.5,
$$
\mathrm{FPR}_a = 1 \times 0.25 \times 0.8 = 0.2, \qquad \mathrm{FPR}_b = 0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.8 = 0.05.
$$
The negatives of group $a$ are wrongly flagged four times as often. Equal false-positive rates would need a different threshold per group, and then the precisions or the false-negative rates would differ. Which criterion matters is a decision about the application, not a property of the model.
:::

There are three places to act on a disparity: before training (reweighting the groups), during training (a constraint in the loss), and after training (one threshold per group, the post-processing of Hardt and coauthors). Deleting the attribute $A$ from the features is not enough when other features are correlated with it.

```python
import pandas as pd
res = pd.DataFrame({"y": y_test, "yhat": model.predict(X_test), "group": X_test["sex"]})
for g, d in res.groupby("group"):                       # held-out predictions only
    pos, neg = d.y == 1, d.y == 0
    print(g, len(d), "positive rate", d.yhat.mean(),
          "TPR", d.yhat[pos].mean(), "FPR", d.yhat[neg].mean(), "PPV", d.y[d.yhat == 1].mean())
```

### 4.9. Comparing two models honestly (self-study) {#model-comparison}

"Model B beats model A by 0.8 points" is a claim about risks, made from noisy estimates. This section, read after session 7, gives the tools to check such a claim before writing it.

**Paired comparisons over folds or seeds.** Evaluate both models on the same folds, or with the same seeds, and work with the differences $\delta_j = s_j(B) - s_j(A)$ for $j = 1, \dots, k$. With $\bar\delta$ their mean and $s_\delta$ their standard deviation, the paired statistic
$$
t = \frac{\bar\delta}{s_\delta/\sqrt{k}}
$$
is compared with a Student distribution with $k - 1$ degrees of freedom. Pairing removes the variation that both models share: an easy fold is easy for both. Two caveats:

-   cross-validation folds share training data, so the differences are correlated and the plain test is too optimistic. Nadeau and Bengio (2003) correct it by replacing $1/k$ with $1/k + n_{\text{test}}/n_{\text{train}}$ in the variance;
-   with few folds or skewed differences, the **Wilcoxon signed-rank test**, which uses only the signed ranks of the differences, makes no normality assumption.

**One test set: McNemar's test.** When both models are evaluated once on the same test examples, only their disagreements matter. Let $n_{01}$ count the examples that A gets right and B gets wrong, and $n_{10}$ the reverse. If both models have the same accuracy, each disagreement goes either way with probability 1/2, and
$$
\chi^2 = \frac{(|n_{01} - n_{10}| - 1)^2}{n_{01} + n_{10}}
$$
approximately follows a $\chi^2$ law with one degree of freedom: reject equality at 5 % above 3.84. With few disagreements, use the exact binomial test instead (Dietterich, 1998).

**An interval for one accuracy: Clopper–Pearson.** If $k$ of $n$ test examples are classified correctly, the exact 95 % interval for the accuracy is
$$
\big[\,B_{0.025}(k,\ n - k + 1),\ \ B_{0.975}(k + 1,\ n - k)\,\big],
$$
where $B_q(a, b)$ is the $q$-quantile of the Beta distribution with parameters $a$ and $b$. For 870 correct answers out of 1000, it gives $[0.848, 0.890]$. The interval is 4 points wide, so a 1-point difference between two models needs the paired tests above, not two overlapping intervals.

**Many comparisons: Bonferroni.** Testing $m$ hypotheses (ten datasets, five baselines) at level $\alpha$ each produces false discoveries. Testing each at level $\alpha/m$ keeps the probability of any false discovery below $\alpha$, by the union bound.

::: note
[A protocol for a claim of improvement]{.tag}

-   **Retrain the baseline** with the same pipeline, split and tuning budget as the new model, instead of copying a number from a paper.
-   **Use at least 3 seeds**, or the folds of 4.2, for each model; report the mean, the standard deviation and the paired test.
-   **Ablate**: remove each new component in turn and measure the loss, so that the gain is attributed.
-   **Touch the test set once**, after every choice is made (4.2).
:::

## 5. Kernels and RKHS {#ch5}

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Positive definite kernel]{.tag} $k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a positive definite kernel if there exists a map $\phi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}$ (a Hilbert space) such that
$$
k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x')\rangle.
$$
Equivalent: for every $n$, every $(x_i)$ and every $(c_i) \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
\sum_{ij} c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) \geq 0
$$
— the Gram matrix $K = (k(x_i, x_j))$ is symmetric positive.
:::

::: ex
[Examples]{.tag}

-   **Polynomial** $k(x,x') = (\langle x,x'\rangle + c)^p$ (explicit feature map: all monomials of degree $\leq p$, dimension $\binom{d+p}{p}$).
-   **Gaussian (RBF)** $k(x,x') = \exp(-\gamma\|x - x'\|^2)$ — feature map of infinite dimension: expanding
    $$
    e^{2\gamma\langle x,x'\rangle}e^{-\gamma\|x\|^2}e^{-\gamma\|x'\|^2}
    $$
    as a power series in $\langle x, x'\rangle$ exhibits $\phi(x)$ = a renormalized Gaussian vector.
-   **On graphs**: the diffusion kernel between nodes, $k(u, v) = [e^{-\beta L}]_{uv}$, with the graph Laplacian $L = D - A$ (degree matrix minus adjacency matrix, cf. Graph ML module), or the *shortest-path kernel* — kernels are the ancestor of GNNs!
:::

### 5.1. The Moore-Aronszajn theorem

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Moore-Aronszajn (sketch)]{.tag} If $k$ is a positive definite kernel, there exists a unique Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of functions $\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that

-   **(i)** $k_x := k(\cdot, x) \in \mathcal{H}$ for every $x$, and
-   **(ii)** the *reproducing property*: $f(x) = \langle f, k_x\rangle$ for every $f \in \mathcal{H}$, every $x$.

It is called the RKHS of $k$.

::: proof
*Construction.* Set $\mathcal{H}_0 = \mathrm{Span}\{k_x : x \in \mathcal{X}\}$ (finite combinations) and, for $f = \sum_i \alpha_i k_{x_i}$, $g = \sum_j \beta_j k_{y_j}$,
$$
\langle f, g\rangle_0 := \sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\beta_j\, k(x_i, y_j).
$$
This form is well defined (independent of the decompositions: reduce to the case $\langle k_x, k_y\rangle_0 = k(x,y)$ and expand), bilinear, and positive by the very definition of a positive definite kernel. Definiteness follows from Cauchy-Schwarz:
$$
|f(x)|^2 = |\langle f, k_x\rangle_0|^2 \leq \|f\|_0^2\, k(x,x).
$$

*Completion.* This inequality above all shows that the evaluation $f \mapsto f(x)$ is 1-Lipschitz-continuous on $\mathcal{H}_0$: it extends to the completion $\mathcal{H}$, whose elements are therefore genuine *functions* (local uniform limits of elements of $\mathcal{H}_0$). The reproducing property, true on $\mathcal{H}_0$ by construction, passes to the limit; uniqueness follows from the density of the $k_x$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 5.2. The representer theorem and kernel regression

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Representer theorem]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the RKHS of $k$ and
$$
\hat f \in \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \tfrac1n\sum_i \ell(f(x_i), y_i) + \lambda\|f\|_\mathcal{H}^2
$$
for an arbitrary convex loss. Then $\hat f \in \mathrm{Span}\{k_{x_i} : i \leq n\}$:
$$
\hat f = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\, k(\cdot, x_i).
$$

::: proof
Decompose $\mathcal{H} = V \oplus V^\perp$ with $V = \mathrm{Span}\{k_{x_i}\}$, and $f = f_V + f_\perp$. The reproducing property gives
$$
f(x_i) = \langle f, k_{x_i}\rangle = \langle f_V, k_{x_i}\rangle = f_V(x_i):
$$
the loss term sees only $f_V$. Since $\|f\|^2 = \|f_V\|^2 + \|f_\perp\|^2$, any nonzero orthogonal component costs norm without changing anything on the data: the optimum lies in $V$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Kernel ridge regression (KRR): closed formula]{.tag} The minimizer in $\mathcal{H}$ of
$$
\tfrac1n\sum_i (y_i - f(x_i))^2 + \lambda\|f\|_\mathcal{H}^2
$$
is $\hat f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i k(x_i, x)$ where
$$
\alpha = (K + n\lambda I_n)^{-1} y, \qquad K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j).
$$

::: proof
By the representer theorem, substitute $f = \sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot,x_i)$. The empirical risk becomes $\tfrac1n\|y - K\alpha\|^2$ and
$$
\|f\|_\mathcal{H}^2 = \sum_{ij}\alpha_i\alpha_j k(x_i,x_j) = \alpha^\top K\alpha.
$$
Minimize
$$
\tfrac1n\|y - K\alpha\|^2 + \lambda\,\alpha^\top K\alpha
$$
in $\alpha$; the gradient
$$
\tfrac2n K(K\alpha - y) + 2\lambda K\alpha = 0
$$
factors through $K$ (symmetric): $(K + n\lambda I)\alpha = y$, invertible since $K \succeq 0$.[∎]{.qed}
:::

KRR is to kernels what ridge is to the linear case — in infinite dimension but with only $n$ active degrees of freedom. The SVM of chapter 3 is its "hinge" analogue: the representer theorem justifies *a posteriori* the form $\theta = \sum_i\alpha_i y'_i \phi(x_i)$ obtained by duality.
::::

::: note
[The kernel trick — and its limit]{.tag} Replacing $\langle x_i, x_j\rangle$ by $k(x_i, x_j)$ in the SVM dual = working in an infinite-dimensional space without ever computing $\phi$ (it suffices that $k$ be directly computable: strings, graphs, sequences...).

Powerful, but costly in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ memory and $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ computation: it is this dimensional limit that motivated deep learning (cf. Deep Learning module), which learns *the* representation $\phi$ instead of fixing it.
:::

## 6. Trees, forests, boosting {#ch6}

### 6.1. Decision trees (CART)

Recursive partition of $\mathcal{X}$ by axis-aligned cuts (binary questions "$x_j \leq t$?"). At each leaf, one predicts the mean (regression) or the majority class (classification). Growth: at each node, choose $(j, t)$ maximizing the impurity gain; then **pruning** to avoid overfitting. The exact impurity criteria, for a node $D$ containing the classes in proportions $p_1, \dots, p_K$:

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Usual impurities]{.tag}
$$
\text{entropy: } H(D) = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \log_2 p_k, \qquad \text{Gini: } G(D) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2 = \sum_k p_k(1 - p_k).
$$
In regression, one uses the squared error
$$
Q(D) = \frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{i \in D}(y_i - \bar y_D)^2.
$$
For a split $D = D_L \cup D_R$, the **gain** is
$$
\Delta(j, t) = I(D) - \frac{|D_L|}{|D|} I(D_L) - \frac{|D_R|}{|D|} I(D_R).
$$
:::

::: note
[Gini and entropy are nearly interchangeable]{.tag} With two classes ($p = p_1 = 1 - p_2$): $G(p) = 2p(1-p)$ and $H(p) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)$.

Both are maximal at $p = 1/2$, zero at $0$ and $1$, and their expansion around $1/2$ coincides to first order:
$$
H(p) = 1 - \frac{2}{\ln 2}(p - \tfrac12)^2 + o\big((p-\tfrac12)^2\big) \qquad\text{and}\qquad G(p) = \frac12 - 2(p - \tfrac12)^2.
$$

CART uses Gini (no logarithm, direct computation); ID3/C4.5 use entropy (information gain). The choice is rarely decisive — *pruning* is. CART's cost-complexity pruning minimizes
$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|\text{leaves}(T)|
$$
over the family of subtrees: yet another fit/complexity trade-off (chapter 8).
:::

### 6.2. Random forests (bagging)

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Bagging reduces variance]{.tag} Let $T_1, \dots, T_B$ be predictors with the same variance $\sigma^2$, pairwise correlation $\rho$. The average $A_B = \frac1B\sum_b T_b$ satisfies $$\mathrm{Var}(A_B) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\,\sigma^2.$$

::: proof
$$
\mathrm{Var}(A_B) = \frac{1}{B^2}\big[\sum_b \mathrm{Var}(T_b) + \sum_{b \neq b'} \mathrm{Cov}(T_b, T_{b'})\big] = \frac{1}{B^2}\big[B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2\big] = \frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{B-1}{B}\rho\sigma^2,
$$
which rewrites as announced. *iid case* ($\rho = 0$, for example Gaussian variables with the same law): $\mathrm{Var} = \sigma^2/B$ — divide the variance by $B$ by averaging independent replicates.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why it works so well for trees]{.tag} As $B \to \infty$, the residual variance tends toward the floor $\rho\sigma^2$: the whole art consists in lowering $\rho$. Random forests combine two mechanisms: (i) the **bootstrap** (resampling the rows); (ii) the random selection of $m_{\text{try}} < d$ candidate variables at each split (*decorrelation*), which forces the trees to differ structurally. Unpruned trees have low bias and high variance — exactly the profile that bagging can correct.

Bonus: each tree leaves out on average $e^{-1} \approx 37\%$ of the data (out-of-bag), so every example can be predicted by the trees that never saw it. This gives a *free* risk estimate, a cheap complement to the cross-validation of chapter 4 (`oob_score=True` in the code below). Forests remain a hard-to-beat *tabular* baseline.
:::

### 6.3. Boosting: gradient descent in function space

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — The functional problem]{.tag} One seeks $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ minimizing $$\Phi(f) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell\big(f(x_i), y_i\big),$$ where $\ell(\hat y, y)$ is convex and differentiable in the prediction $\hat y$ (quadratic, logistic...). One builds $f$ as a sum $f_M = \sum_{m=0}^M \eta\, h_m$ of simple functions (typically small trees), chosen one at a time — a stagewise *additive model*.
:::

:::: thm
